'''''Crataegus monogyna''''', known as '''common hawthorn''', '''whitethorn,''' '''one-seed hawthorn''', or '''single-seeded hawthorn''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the rose family, [[Rosaceae]]. It grows to about {{Convert|10|m|abbr=off}} tall, producing [[plant sexuality|hermaphrodite]] flowers in late spring. The berry-like [[pome]]s (known as haws) contain a stone-encased seed.

The plant is native to Europe, but has been introduced in many other parts of the world. The pome flesh is of little culinary interest due to its dryness, but is used to make jellies. The young leaves and petals are also edible.

==Description==
The common hawthorn is a [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] up to about {{Convert|10|m|abbr=off}} tall,<ref name="Bean's Trees and Shrubs">{{cite web |work=Bean's Trees and Shrubs |publisher=International Dendrology Society |title=Crataegus monogyna Jacq. |url=http://www.beanstreesandshrubs.org/browse/crataegus/crataegus-monogyna-jacq/| access-date = 5 November 2021}}</ref> with a dense crown. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is dull brown with vertical orange cracks. The younger stems bear sharp thorns, about {{Convert|12.5|mm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long. The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|20 to 40|mm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, [[obovate]], and deeply lobed, sometimes almost to the midrib, with the lobes spreading at a wide angle. The upper surface is dark green above and paler underneath.<ref name="Bean's Trees and Shrubs" />

The [[hermaphrodite]] flowers are produced in late spring (May to early June in its native area) in [[corymb]]s of 5–25 together; they have numerous red [[stamen]]s and a single [[Style (botany)|style]] and are moderately fragrant. The flowers are white, frequently pink.<ref name="Parnell-2012">{{cite book |author1=Parnell, J. |author2=Curtis, T. |author3=Webb, D.A. |year=2012 |title=Webb's an Irish Flora |publisher=[[Cork University Press]] |isbn=978-185918-4783}}</ref> They are pollinated by [[midge]]s, bees, and other insects, and later in the year bear numerous haws. The haw is a small, oval, dark red [[fruit]] about {{cvt|10|mm}} long, [[Berry (botany)|berry]]-like, but structurally a [[pome]] containing a single [[seed]] within a stone, the [[pyrena|pyrene]].<ref name="Bean's Trees and Shrubs" /> The haws develop in groups of two or three along smaller branches. They are pulpy and delicate in taste.

Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 107.3 days, and bears an average of 2.8 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 75.7% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 9.0% [[carbohydrate]]s and 1.0% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

===Similar species===
The common hawthorn is distinguished from the related but less widespread [[Midland hawthorn]] (''C. laevigata'') by its more upright growth, the leaves being deeply lobed, with spreading lobes, and the flowers having just one style, not two or three. They are interfertile, however, so hybrids occur frequently; they are only entirely distinct in their more typical forms. Another species that also hybridises with the common hawthorn is ''[[Crataegus rhipidophylla]]'', which is distinguished by having finely instead of coarsely serrated lobe margins.

The pomes of some other hawthorns may have up to five seeds.

== Taxonomy ==
This species is one of several that have been referred to as ''[[Crataegus oxyacantha]]'', a name that has been rejected by the botanical community as too ambiguous. In 1793, [[Friedrich Kasimir Medikus|Medikus]] published the name ''C. apiifolia'' for a European hawthorn now included in ''C. monogyna,'' but that name is [[Nomen illegitimum|illegitimate]] under the rules of [[botanical nomenclature]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Christensen |first=Knud Ib |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vz0lAQAAMAAJ |title=Revision of ''Crataegus'' sect. ''Crataegus'' and nothosect. ''Crataeguineae'' (Rosaceae-Maloideae) in the Old World |publisher=American Society of Plant Taxonomists |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-912861-35-7}}</ref><ref name="IPNI">{{cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |title=Crataegus apiifolia |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/67864-2 |website=[[International Plant Names Index]] |publisher= |quote=}}</ref>

Other common names include '''may''', '''mayblossom''', '''maythorn''', (as the plant generally flowers in May) '''quickthorn''', '''whitethorn''', '''motherdie''', and '''haw'''.<ref name="CABI">{{Cite journal
 |last1= Pasiecznik |first1= N |date= 2022 |title= Crataegus monogyna (hawthorn). |journal= CABI Compendium |publisher= CABI International |doi= 10.1079/cabicompendium |url= https://doi.org/10.1079/cabicompendium.16496|url-access= subscription }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Ripon Parks 4 June 2023 (50).JPG|thumb|Flowers, [[North Yorkshire]], England]]

The common hawthorn is native to Europe,<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021" /> being found in Ireland and Britain.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968 "Excursion Flora of the British Isles." Cambridge University Press.{{ISBN|0 521 04656 4}}</ref> It is also found in northwestern Africa and Western Asia,<ref name="CABI"/> and has become naturalised in the [[Pacific Northwest]] in North America.<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |page=240}}</ref>

It grows in [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed]], semi-cleared areas.<ref name="tktimb" />

==Ecology==

Haws are important for [[wildlife]] in winter, particularly [[thrush (bird)|thrushes]] and [[waxwing]]s; these birds eat the haws and disperse the [[seed]]s in their droppings.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/plants/top-10-plants-for-birds/ | title=Top 10 Plants for Birds | publisher=Immediate Media Company Ltd. | work=[[BBC Gardeners' World]] | date=20 September 2019 | access-date=30 September 2024}}</ref>

Due to excessive animal grazing in the area, new shoots of vulnerable ''C. monogyna'' trees in the open field are eaten by animals. This does not allow them to grow and causes them to take a horizontally irregular shape on the ground.<ref>{{Cite web |title=RikenMon's Nature.Guide {{!}} Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) |url=https://nature.guide/card.aspx?lang=en&id=1218 |access-date=2024-10-02 |website=nature.guide}}</ref>

A study in Wales indicated that current levels of [[overgrazing]] by sheep might extirpate the species in 60–70 years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Good |first1=J. E. G. |last2=Bryant |first2=R. |last3=Carlill |first3=P. |date=1990 |title=Distribution, Longevity and Survival of Upland Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) Scrub in North Wales in Relation to Sheep Grazing |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=272–283 |doi=10.2307/2403584 |jstor=2403584 |bibcode=1990JApEc..27..272G |issn=0021-8901}}</ref>

== Uses ==
=== Food ===
The fruit of hawthorn, called haws, are sometimes said to be edible raw,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Juan |last2=Chai |first2=Xiaoyun |last3=Zhao |first3=Fenglan |last4=Hou |first4=Guige |last5=Meng |first5=Qingguo |date=2022-09-15 |title=Food Applications and Potential Health Benefits of Hawthorn |journal=Foods |language=en |volume=11 |issue=18 |page=2861 |doi=10.3390/foods11182861 |issn=2304-8158 |pmc=9498108 |pmid=36140986 |doi-access=free}}</ref> but are too dry to be of interest.<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=13}}</ref> They are commonly made into jellies,<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021" /> jams, syrups, or wine, or to add flavour to brandy.

The young leaves are tender enough to be used in salads.<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021" /><ref>Mabey, Richard (2001). ''Food for Free'', Collins.</ref> The petals are also edible.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Crataegus monogyna'' |url=http://www.survival.org.au/bf_crataegus_monogyna.php |access-date=9 September 2011 |work=Survival and Self Sufficiency}}</ref> Hawthorn petals are used in the medieval English recipe for spinee, an [[almond milk]]-based [[pottage]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Foods of England |url=https://foodsofengland.info/spinee.html |access-date=21 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{citation |author=Jaine, T. |title=Oxford Symposium on Food & Cookery, 1986: The Cooking Medium: Proceedings |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ohdhy5fiYbwC |year=1987 |publisher=Prospect Books |isbn=978-0-907325-36-9}} p. 70</ref> recorded in ''[[The Forme of Cury]]'' by the head chef of King [[Richard II]], {{Circa|1390}}.

=== Medicine ===
[[File:2013-05-23 07 24 06 Crataegus monogyna 'Crimson Cloud' blossoms in Elko Nevada.jpg|thumb|'Crimson Cloud' in [[Elko, Nevada|Elko]], Nevada]]

''C. monogyna'' is one of the most common species used as the "hawthorn" of traditional [[herbalism]]. The plant parts used are usually sprigs with both leaves and flowers, or alternatively the fruit ("berries").<ref name="UniMarylandMedCtr">{{citation |chapter-url=http://umm.edu/health/medical/altmed/herb/hawthorn |title=University of Maryland Medical Center: Complementary and Alternative Medicine Guide |chapter=Hawthorn |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170630225231/http://umm.edu/health/medical/altmed/herb/hawthorn |access-date=3 October 2016|archive-date=2017-06-30}}</ref> Hawthorn has been investigated by [[evidence-based medicine]] for treating cardiac insufficiency.<ref name="UniMarylandMedCtr" />

''C. monogyna'' is a source of [[antioxidant]] [[phytochemical]]s, especially extracts of hawthorn leaves with flowers.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Oztürk N, Tunçel M |title=Assessment of Phenolic Acid Content and In Vitro Antiradical Characteristics of Hawthorn |journal=J Med Food |date=2011 |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=664–669 |doi=10.1089/jmf.2010.0063 |pmid=21554133}}</ref>

===Gardening and agriculture===
{{One source|section|date=September 2023}}

Common hawthorn is extensively planted as a [[hedge]] plant, especially for [[agricultural]] use. Its spines and close branching habit render it effectively livestock- and human-proof, with some basic maintenance. The traditional practice of [[hedgelaying]] is most commonly practised with this species. It is a good [[firewood]], which burns with a good heat and little smoke.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scoutbase.org.uk/library/hqdocs/facts/pdfs/fs315001.pdf |title=The burning properties of wood |publisher=Scouts|access-date=2010-11-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121223202805/http://www.scoutbase.org.uk/library/hqdocs/facts/pdfs/fs315001.pdf|archive-date=2012-12-23}}</ref>

Numerous [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]s exist, some of which are used as garden shrubs. The most widely used hybrid is ''[[Crataegus × media|C. × media]]'' (''C. monogyna'' × ''C. laevigata''), of which several [[cultivar]]s are known, including the very popular 'Paul's Scarlet' with dark pink double flowers. Other garden shrubs that have sometimes been suggested as possible hybrids involving the common hawthorn,{{Citation needed|reason=who has suggested that C. heterophylla is a hybrid?|date=September 2009}} include the [[various-leaved hawthorn]] of the [[Caucasus]], which is only very occasionally found in parks and gardens.

== In culture ==
In pre-modern Europe, hawthorn was used as a symbol of hope, and also as a charm against [[witchcraft]] and [[vampire]]s.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=295}} Hawthorn was believed by some to have the ability to inhibit intruding [[supernatural]] forces, and was also thought to be sacred in nature due to an association between the hawthorn bush and the [[crown of thorns]] that, according to the [[New Testament]], was placed on [[Jesus]].{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=296}}

As protection against witchcraft, hawthorn was sometimes placed in the cradles of infants, or around houses and doorways.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=295}} The Greeks reportedly placed pieces of hawthorn in [[casement window]]s to prevent witches from entering houses,{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=295–296}} while [[Bohemia]]ns placed hawthorn on the thresholds of [[cow house]]s for the same purpose.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=296}} Hawthorn was sometimes placed on the coffin of a deceased person, on top of the person's corpse, or in the corpse's sock.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=296}} In Bosnia, women would sometimes place a piece of hawthorn behind the headcloth of a recently deceased person, and then throw away the remaining twig on their way home.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=296}} If the deceased person was a vampire, it would focus its attention on the hawthorn instead of following the woman home.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=296}} Among the [[South Slavs]], stakes made of hawthorn or [[blackthorn]] wood were considered effective in impaling vampires.{{sfn|Melton|1994|p=297}}

=== Notable trees ===
[[File:Hawthorn St Mars 2.jpg|thumb|The Saint-Mars tree]]

An ancient specimen, and reputedly the oldest tree of any species in France, is to be found alongside the church at [[Saint Mars sur la Futaie]], [[Mayenne]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Common Hawthorn next to the church in Saint-Mars-sur-la-Futaie, Mayenne, France |url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/fra/mayenne/saintmarssurlafutaie/2810_church |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519080238/https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/fra/mayenne/saintmarssurlafutaie/2810_church/ |archive-date=2023-05-19 |website=Monumental trees}}</ref> As of 2009, the tree had a height of {{convert|9|m|ft|abbr=on}} and a girth of {{convert|2.65|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}. The inscription on the plaque beneath reads: "This hawthorn is probably the oldest tree in France. Its origin goes back to [[Julian of Le Mans|St Julien]] (third century)"; this has not yet been verified.

A famous specimen in England was the [[Glastonbury Thorn|Glastonbury or Holy Thorn]] which, according to legend, sprouted from the staff of [[Joseph of Arimathea]] after he thrust it into the ground while visiting Glastonbury in the first century AD. The tree was noteworthy because it flowered twice in a year, once in the late spring which is normal, but also once after the harshness of midwinter had passed. The original tree at Glastonbury Abbey, felled in the 1640s during the [[English Civil War]],<ref name="BBC News-2012">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/magazine-17589575 |title=BBC News – The mystery over who attacked the Holy Thorn Tree |work=[[BBC News]] |date=2012-04-04 |access-date=2014-03-15}}</ref> has been propagated as the cultivar 'Biflora'.<ref>Phipps, J.B.; O'Kennon, R.J.; Lance, R.W. 2003. ''Hawthorns and medlars''. Royal Horticultural Society, Cambridge, UK.</ref> A replacement was planted by the local council in 1951, but was truncated by vandals in 2010.<ref name="BBC News-2012" />

The oldest known living specimen in [[East Anglia]], and possibly in the United Kingdom, is known as the [[Hethel Old Thorn]],<ref name="Wildlifetrusts.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.wildlifetrust.org.uk/norfolk/nature%20reserves/map-links/hethel.htm |title=Hethel Old Thorn |publisher=Wildlifetrusts.org/ |access-date=18 February 2007 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070224040329/http://www.wildlifetrust.org.uk/norfolk/nature%20reserves/map-links/hethel.htm |archive-date=24 February 2007}}</ref> and is located in the churchyard in the small village of [[Hethel]], south of Norwich, in Norfolk.  It is reputed to be more than 700 years old, having been planted in the thirteenth century.<ref name="Wildlifetrusts.org"/>
